newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurobourses slip - eye Sunday's french poll.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurobourses slip - eye Sunday's french poll.

text.p: Major European bourses slipped on Friday but the dollar benefitted as investors, nervous about the future of European Monetary Union, anxously awaited the outcome of Sunday's French elections.

The dollar remained in favour as plans for a 1999 launch of the euro -- and the strength of the currency if it is launched -- were thrown further into doubt by the clash between Bonn and the Bundesbank this week and what is perceived as an increase in the the possibility that the opposition socialists could win power in France.
Frankfurt shares had tumbled by about 1.5 percent by mid-morning as German markets reacted to the row over revaluing German gold assets after their holiday on Thursday.

On the Paris bourse, leading stocks, which have suffered badly from election jitters over the past few days, shed more than 1.5 percent within the first 10 minutes of trading, though they recovered a good portion of these loses later.

"Once again, a number of people are coming round to a probable Socialist victory," said a broker. The publication of an opinion poll in the daily Le Parisien this morning "gave a little extra help," he added.

Some professionals were eyeing 2,500 on the main CAC index as a trading target for Friday, on a view that if the market settled at that level, it would be positioned for Monday and any fall on a Socialist win would be limited. The index was at about 2565 at 0900 gmt.
In London blue chips opened moderately higher but soon fell back into negative territory with trading volumes kept thin, analysts said, by uncertainly over France and EMU.
The FTSE 100 index was down about a quarter percent by mid-morning despite a firmer bond market and the upcoming flotation of the Halifax Building Society.

"If the Socialists win (in France) there is bound to be a knee-jerk reaction in French and German bond and share markets on Monday which will spill over into our market," the head of trading at a major London brokerage said.
The listing on Monday of the Halifax, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, should prop up the financial sector helping to limit the downside, he said.
"The institutions have to have Halifax in their portfolios and the market knows it," the trader said, "But even that won't be enough to keep the FTSE afloat if the EMU turmoil continues."

On the foreign exchange front the dollar (along with sterling) continued to be supported by its role as a safe-haven currency. By 0900 GMT it was trading at 1.705 marks, up from 1.6990 in late Europe on Thursday. Against the yen, the dollar was trading at 116.30 yen against 116.12 late Thursday.

"The problems between the Bundesbank and the German government continue," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston, adding that he expected pressure for German Finance Minister Theo Waigle's resignation to mount.
The dollar is set to benefit as as long as the German gold revaluation plan, which would help Germany cut back its deficits to make the grade for EMU, remains an issue, said analysts.

"There's a lot of uncertainties concerning the gold and currency valuation plan of the Bundesbank...But we still have to wait for a vote in the lower house in Germany which intends to change the Bundesbank law," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank.
CURRENCIES AT 0900 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.705 marks and 116.30 yen compared with 1.6990 marks and 116.12 yen in late European trading on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0900 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 16 points at 4,656.3
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 14 points at 2,565.1.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 52 points at 3583.
PRECIOUS METALS Gold was firmer at $345.50 versus a London close on Thursday of $344.05. Silver was also firmer at $4.84.
